a-.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin ad-, from the preposition ad (“to, towards”).

abate.etymology: From Italian abate, from Late Latin abbās, abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Compare Campidanese abati.

abba.etymology: From Latin aqua. Compare with the Campidanese àcua phonetic variation. Compare also with the Romanian apă.

de.etymology: Inherited from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *de.

in.etymology: From Latin in, from earlier en, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).

glosses_en: used before epithets, describing the person being addressed, for emphasis; you
o.etymology: From Italian o (“or”), from Latin aut (“or”), from Proto-Italic *auti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewti (“on the other hand”), derived from *h₂ew (“away from, off”). Doublet of a.

glosses_en: plural of su: the (masculine plural definite article)
plural of sa: the (feminine plural definite article)
is.etymology: From syllabic apocope of issos, issas, from Latin ipsōs, ipsās, masculine and feminine accusative plural forms of ipse (“himself”).

Canada.etymology: Borrowed from English and French Canada, from Laurentian kanata (“village, settlement”).

glosses_en: Malta (an archipelago and country in Southern Europe, in the Mediterranean Sea)
Malta (the largest island in the Maltese Archipelago)

eo.etymology: From Latin egō, from Proto-Italic *egō, from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂. Compare Italian io, Sicilian iu.

glosses_en: alternative form of a, sometimes used before vowels

banana.etymology: From Spanish banana, from Wolof banaana.

cane.etymology: From Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Italian cane.

male.etymology: From Latin male. Compare Italian male.

glosses_en: first-person singular present indicative of èssere

mama.etymology: From Latin mamma, from Ancient Greek μάμμη (mámmē).

chin.etymology:
From Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”). The shift -u- → -i- is probably due to analogy with in.
Compare Logudorese and Campidanese cun, Italian con, Portuguese com, Spanis

e.etymology: From Latin et, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *éti.

mare.etymology: From Latin mare. Compare Italian mare.

essere.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse.

tres.etymology: From Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

mela.etymology: From Late Latin mēla, from mēlum, from Latin mālum.

noi.etymology: Inherited from Latin novem. Compare Italian nove.

who, whom, which (nominative and accusative case)
chi.etymology: From Latin quid, from Proto-Italic *kʷid, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid.

ape.etymology: From Latin apis, apem. Compare Logudorese abe, Campidanese abi.

patata.etymology: From Spanish patata, from Taíno batata.

glosses_en: third-person singular present indicative of èssere
est.etymology: From Latin est, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti.

rosa.etymology: From Latin rosa, of disputed origin.

body (fleshly or corporeal nature of a human)
body (any physical object or material thing)
body (organisation, company or other authoritative group)
corpus.etymology: From Latin corpus, from Proto-Italic *korpos, from Proto-Indo-European *krépos ~ *krépesos, derived from the root *krep- (“body”). Compare English riff.

cabra.etymology: From Latin capra, from caper, from Proto-Indo-European *kápros.

vos.etymology: From Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, from the oblique case forms of Proto-Indo-European *yúHs (“you”).

nos.etymology: From Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs, from the oblique case forms of Proto-Indo-European *wéy (“we”).

luna.etymology: From Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂.

latte.etymology: From Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac.

bos.etymology: From Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, from the oblique case forms of Proto-Indo-European *yúHs (“you”).

manu.etymology: From Latin manus. Compare Catalan mà, French main, Galician man, Italian mano, Occitan man, Portuguese mão, Romanian mână, Spanish mano.

oca.etymology: From Late Latin auca, syncope of *avica, from classical Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Catalan, Spanish, Venetan, and Sicilian oca, French oie, Occitan auca, Romansh auca, ocha, Friulian ocje, Dalmatian jauca.

biu.etymology: From Latin vivus. Compare Italian vivo.

ibi.etymology: From Latin ibi. Found in various Nuorese-speaking towns, along with the variant ibe.

sa.etymology: From Latin ipsa (“herself”), feminine of ipse (“himself”).

linna.etymology: From Latin ligna, plural of lignum, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-no- (“that which is collected”), from *leǵ-.

pasta.etymology: From Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).

che.etymology: From a contraction of Old Logudorese co e (“as, like”), from Latin quō(modo) et.

domo.etymology: From Latin domus (“house”), from Proto-Italic *domos, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, derived from the root *dem- (“to build”).

mesa.etymology: From Vulgar Latin mēsa, from Latin mēnsa.

semper.etymology: From Latin semper, whose first element is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *sḗm (“one”).

stella.etymology: From Latin stēlla, from Proto-Italic *stērlā, a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr, derived from the root *h₂eh₁s- (“to burn”).

glosses_en: China (a cultural region and civilization in East Asia, occupying the region around the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl Rivers, taken as a whole under its various dynasties)
China (a large country in East Asia, occupying the region around the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl Rivers; the People's Republic of China, since 1949)

ballare.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ballare, from Late Latin ballāre. The Campidanese variant baddai represents the native holdout in a sea of Italianisms.

bene.etymology: From Latin bene (“well”). Compare Italian bene.

aba.etymology: From Latin ava, feminine of avus.

su.etymology: From Latin ipsum, accusative singular of ipse (“himself”).

ou.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin ōvum, possibly via Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum.

sue.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin sūs, suem (“pig”), from Proto-Italic *sūs, derived from Proto-Indo-European *suH- (“pig, hog, swine”). Compare Nuorese sughe, Sassarese sua (dialectal sui).

una.etymology: Inherited from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus.

feu.etymology: Ultimately from Latin foedus. Compare Spanish feo.

glosses_en: apocopic form of de used before a vowel
ortographic realization of a [d] sound in certain environments

mesu.etymology: From a cross of Latin mēnsus (“measured, distributed”) and medius (“middle, half”). Like Dalmatian mesu and perhaps Venetan miso; unlike Italian mezzo and Romanian miez.

lei.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish ley, from Latin lex, legem.

mere.etymology: From the nominative of Latin maior (“greater, elder”), via intermediate forms like *maire, *meire. For final /-or/ > /-re/, cf. Sardinian sorre, from Latin soror (“sister”).

core.etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

mente.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin mēns, mentem (“mind; intellect, thought”), from Proto-Italic *mentis, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”). Compare Campidanese menti.

mille.etymology: From Latin mille, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂. Cognates include Italian mille and French mille.

affogare.etymology: Borrowed from Italian affogare or Catalan afogar; either way from Vulgar Latin *affōcāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre.

essi.etymology: From Latin esse, present infinitive of sum (“to be”).

beni.etymology: From Latin bene (“well”). Compare Italian bene.

burdo.etymology: From Late Latin burdus (“bastard, mule”), probably of Celtic origin.

pensare.etymology: From Latin pēnsāre (“weigh carefully”), frequentative of pendere.

frore.etymology: From earlier *flore, from Latin flōrem, accusative singular of flōs (“flower”), from Proto-Italic *flōs (accusative *flōzem), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃s (“flower, blossom”), derived from the root *bʰleh₃- (“to bloom”).

morte.etymology: From Latin mors, mortem. Compare Italian morte.

glosses_en: Attached to a stem, forms the present infinitive of most regular verbs
-are.etymology: From Latin -āre, present infinitive of -ō (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix), from Proto-Italic *-āō. Compare Campidanese -ai.

how (used as a modifier to indicate surprise, delight, or other strong feelings)

nura.etymology: From Late Latin nura, from Latin nurus, from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

oro.etymology: Borrowed from Italian oro, from Latin aurum.

ses.etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Italic *seks, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

aici.etymology: From Catalan així, from Old Occitan aissi, from Latin eccum sīc.

gattu.etymology: From Latin cattus. Cognates include Italian gatto and Spanish gato.

glosses_en: Ukraine (a country in Eastern Europe, bordering on the north shore of the Black Sea)

frutta.etymology: From Late Latin fructa, from Latin fructus.

mata.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish, perhaps from Late Latin matta.

jaja.etymology: From Spanish yaya (“grandma”), or from Greek γιαγιά (giagiá, “grandmother”).

vida.etymology: From Latin vīta. Cf. Spanish vida.

deo.etymology: From Latin ego, from Proto-Italic *egō, from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂.

mari.etymology: From Latin mare. Compare Italian mare.

a.etymology: From Latin ac, alternative form of atque (“and, and also; as, then”).

mali.etymology: From Latin male. Compare Italian male.

como.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum modo. Compare Romanian acum.

abe.etymology: From Latin apis, apem. Compare Campidanese abi, Nuorese ape.

glosses_en: to me (first person singular dative pronoun)

èssere.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. Forms beginning with f- apparently come from Latin fierī.

edu.etymology: From Latin haedus, from Proto-Italic *haidos, probably a loanword from a pre-Indo-European substrate language due to the fact that it cannot be derived from any known root. The only sure cognate is Proto-Germanic *gaits (“goat”). Compare Ar

sera.etymology: From Late Latin sēra, from ellipsis of Latin sēra diēs, from sērus (“late”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-ro-. Compare Italian sera, French soir, Venetan séra, Friulian sere, Sicilian sira, Romanian seară, Romansh saira.

abasia.etymology: Borrowed from Italian abasia, derived from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, “step”).

glosses_en: to calm down (to cause to become less excited, intense or angry)
to calm down (to become less intense) (of wind)
abbacare.etymology: Likely a borrowing. Compare Occitan abaucar (“to calm; to calm down”). The northern forms might be from a language of northern Italy (compare Lombard balcà (“to die down, calm down”)). Compare Campidanese abbacai.

unu.etymology: From Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one, single”).

sidi.etymology: From Latin sitis, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“decay; destruction”), derived from the root *dʰgʷʰey- (“to decline; to perish”). Compare Italian sete.

morti.etymology: From Latin mors, mortem. Compare Italian morte.

lagu.etymology: From Latin lacus (“lake”). Compare Aragonese laco, Catalan llac, French lac, Italian lago, Maltese lag, Portuguese lago, Romanian lac, Spanish lago.

cara.etymology: From Spanish cara and/or Catalan cara, both from Late Latin cara, from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára).

duru.etymology: From Latin dūrus. Compare Italian duro.

lunis.etymology: From Latin Lūnae diēs, variant of diēs Lūnae (“day of the moon”).

boi.etymology: From Latin bōs (“cow, bull”). Compare Italian bue.

glosses_en: stall (bench or table on which small articles of merchandise are exposed for sale)
bancu.etymology: From Catalan banc, of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”).

glosses_en: plural of sa: the (feminine plural definite article)
sas.etymology: From Latin ipsās, accusative plural feminine of ipse (“himself”).

glosses_en: bird (in general), especially eagles or other birds of prey
ae.etymology: Inherited from Latin avem, accusative of avis.

iférru.etymology: From Latin īnfernum, neuter form of īnfernus (“of the lower regions”).

sete.etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Italic *septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

prata.etymology: From earlier *plata, from Vulgar Latin *platta, plattus (“flattened”). Compare Spanish Spanish plata.

tue.etymology: From Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Compare Italian tu, Portuguese tu, Spanish tú, French tu, Romanian tu, Aromanian tu, Corsican tù, Catalan tu, Sicilian tu.

amu.etymology: From Latin hamus. Compare Italian amo.

jana.etymology: From Latin Diana, from Proto-Italic *deiwā, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós.

sardu.etymology: Of unclear origin. Possibly from an adjectival derivate of the pre-Roman substrate root *sard- through Latin sardus.

lupu.etymology: Borrowed from Italian lupo. Not inherited from Latin lupus; note the absence of a form like *lubu as well as the absence of the animal itself from the island.

abi.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin apis, apem. Compare Logudorese abe, Nuorese ape.

pira.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular. Compare Italian pera, French poire, Spanish pera.

binti.etymology: From Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Italic *wīgentī, from Proto-Indo-European *wídḱm̥ti, from earlier *dwidḱómt, from *dwi- (“two”) + *déḱm̥t (“ten”).

biri.etymology: From Latin vidēre. Compare Catalan veure.

glosses_en: alternative form of fàghere (“to do; make”)

erba.etymology: From Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).

malu.etymology: From Latin malus. Compare Italian malo.

limba.etymology: From Latin lingua. For the change /ɡʷ/ > /b/, compare Romanian limbă.

muru.etymology: From Latin mūrus. Compare Italian muro.

annu.etymology: From Latin annus. Compare Italian anno.

binu.etymology: From Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“wine; vine”).

nui.etymology: From Latin nūbes. Compare Italian nube and nuvola.

ogu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus. Compare Italian occhio.

oru.etymology: Borrowed from Italian oro, from Latin aurum.

pei.etymology: From Latin pes, pedem. Compare Catalan peu, French pied (foot), Italian piede (foot), Latin pes (foot), Latvian pēda, Lithuanian pėdės, Portuguese pé (foot), Spanish pie (foot).

bentu.etymology: From Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts, from the root *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

beru.etymology: From Latin vērus, from Proto-Italic *wēros, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros, derived from *weh₁- (“true”).

cottu.etymology: From Latin coctus. Compare Italian cotto.

custu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste. Compare Italian questo, Sicilian chistu, Romanian acest, Occitan aqueste, Catalan aquest.

fenu.etymology: From Latin faenum. Compare Italian fieno.

grogu.etymology: Possibly borrowed from Catalan groc, from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).

babbu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *babbus. Compare Italian babbo and Romansh bab.

ossu.etymology: From Latin ossum, from os. Compare Catalan os, French os, Interlingua osso, Italian osso, Portuguese osso, Romanian os, Spanish hueso.

ortu.etymology: From Latin hortus. Compare Italian orto.

issu.etymology: From Latin ipsum, masculine accusative of ipse. Compare with Italian esso, Portuguese isso, Sicilian ssu and Spanish eso.

isula.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *isula, from Latin īnsula. Compare Italian isola.

artu.etymology: From Latin altus. Compare Italian alto.

prumu.etymology: From earlier plumbu, from Latin plumbum (“lead”). Compare Italian Italian piombo.

pranu.etymology: From Latin plānus, compare Italian piano.

prenu.etymology:
From an original *plenu, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), derived from the root *pleh₁- (“to fill”).
Compare Italian pieno, Catalan ple, French plein, Romanian plin and Spanish lleno

prattu.etymology: From an original *plattu, compare Italian piatto.

pranta.etymology: From earlier *planta, from Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

preda.etymology: From Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”).

pramu.etymology: From an original *palmu, from *plamu; compare Italian palmo.

pruppu.etymology: From Latin polypus (“octopus”), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous).

oto.etymology: From Latin octō, from Proto-Italic *oktō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.

pische.etymology: Inherited from Latin piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

mele.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

melone.etymology: From Late Latin mēlō, mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”).

gigante.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin gigās, from Ancient Greek γίγᾱς (gígās, “giant”).

cria.etymology: Deverbal, from Logudorese criare and Campidanese criai (“to lay an egg; to give birth”).

glosses_en: to you (second person singular dative pronoun)
tibi.etymology: From Latin tibi. Found in the towns of Bitti and Orani.

bega.etymology: Possibly a borrowing from Spanish vega. Ultimate origin is unknown, but it is likely akin to Galician veiga and Basque ibai (“river”), ibar (“valley”).

godire.etymology: Borrowed from Italian godere, with a change in conjugation. Synonym and near-doublet of gosare, which arrived via Spanish.

cicogna.etymology: From Latin cicōnia, derived from Proto-Indo-European *kekoh₂n-, from the root *keh₂n- (“to sing”).

piccione.etymology: Borrowed from Italian piccione. Cf. the native synonym columbu.

bufare.etymology: Compare Valencian usage of Catalan bufar.

fusile.etymology: Borrowed from French fusil; see there for further etymology.

labore.etymology: From Latin labor (“work, labor”). Compare to Catalan llavor (“seed”).

luche.etymology: From Latin lūcem, accusative singular of lūx, from Proto-Italic *louks (accusative *loukem), from the Proto-Indo-European *léwks, derived from the root *lewk- (“white; light; bright”). Cognates include Italian luce and Spanish luz.

pintare.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pinctāre. Wagner does not exclude the possibility of the word being borrowed from Spanish pintar, however.

olvidare.etymology: From Spanish olvidar, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, ultimately from Latin oblīvīscī.

padule.etymology: From Late Latin padūlem, from Latin palūd- via metathesis.

sene.etymology: From Latin senem, accusative case form of senex, from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”).

casu.etymology: From Latin cāseus, see there for more. Compare Romanian caș, Spanish queso, Portuguese queijo.

vinu.etymology: From Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“wine; vine”).

glosses_en: Variant first-person singular present indicative of èssere

supre.etymology: From Latin super, influenced by Spanish or Catalan sobre.

logu.etymology: From Latin locus, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).

sessanta.etymology: From Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).

carri.etymology: From Latin carnem, accusative of carō (“flesh”), from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-, *(s)ker- (“to cut”).

caliche.etymology: From Latin calix, calicem, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κύλιξ (kúlix).

pede.etymology: From Latin pes, pedem. Compare Catalan peu, French pied (foot), Italian piede (foot), Latin pes (foot), Latvian pēda, Lithuanian pėdės, Portuguese pé (foot), Spanish pie (foot).

formiga.etymology: From Latin formīca, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *morwi.

cun.etymology: From Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”). Compare Italian con, Portuguese com, Spanish con, Romanian cu, Sicilian cu. Compare also Nuorese chin.

glosses_en: Iceland (an island and country in the North Atlantic Ocean in Europe)
Estonia (a country in northeastern Europe, on the southeastern coast of the Baltic Sea)

pisciare.etymology: From Italian pisciare, displacing the native Sardinian mejare.

rese.etymology: From Latin res (“thing, affair”). Cf. Spanish res (“head of cattle”).

glosses_en: Sardinia (an island and autonomous region of Italy, in the Mediterranean Sea)
Sardigna.etymology: In this form, borrowed from Old Italian Sardigna. The archaic alternative forms were either inherited from Latin or nativised from Italian.

ampulla.etymology: Borrowed from Latin ampulla, derived from amphora.

vostru.etymology: From Latin voster, vostrum, from earlier vester.

abati.etymology: From Italian abate, from Late Latin abbās, abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Compare Logudorese abate.

boxi.etymology: From Latin vōcem, accusative form of vōx, from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs (“voice”, “speech”).

foche.etymology: From Latin fōcem, early monophthongized variant of faucem.

glosses_en: plural of su: the (masculine plural definite article)
sos.etymology: From Latin ipsōs, accusative plural of ipse (“himself”).

sutta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subta, from Latin subtus.

ànima.etymology: From Latin anima, derived from animus (“mind, soul”).

arna.etymology: Cognate with Catalan arna and Occitan arna.

xrebu.etymology: From a metathesis of cerbu, with deaffrication and voicing of the initial /t͡ʃ/.

xebru.etymology: Probably from a metathesis of xrebu, itself derived from a metathesis of cerbu.

xrebru.etymology: Probably from a conflation of xrebu and xebru, both from a metathesis of cerbu.

cérbiu.etymology: Likely from a Late Vulgar Latin *cervius, masculine equivalent of Late Latin cervia (“hind”), derived from Latin cervus (“deer”) (whence Campidanese cerbu).

arvatze.etymology: From Arabic الْبَزّ (al-bazz, “cloth”), perhaps via Old Italian albace, albagio. Compare Campidanese orbaci, and Nuorese orbace.

fròngia.etymology: From Late Latin frondia n pl, a collective noun derived from Classical Latin frondeus (“leafy”). Same source as Old Italian fronza (“leafy branch; green leaf of a wheat plant”), which might have influenced the quality of the stressed vowel

bussica.etymology:
From Italian vescica, vessica and other Italo-Romance variants, from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.
The Italian route of transmission is indicated by the absence, from Logudorese and Campidanese, of any variant with voiced /-ɡ-/.

isfrunza.etymology: Likely related to isvrunciare (“to whip; (figuratively) to reproach”) and frunza (“branch; rod; sprout”).

isvrunciare.etymology: Likely related to isfrunza (“rod, whip”) and frunza (“branch; rod; sprout”). Perhaps partially shaped by influence from Italian broncio (“sulk, pout”).

umprere.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *implĕre~*implīre, from Latin implēre. Cognate with Catalan omplir.

abbabbaluccai.etymology: From an onomatopoeic root bab- also found in Italian babbeo (“idiot, moron”), babbione (“blockhead”).

surbiri.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorbīre, from Latin sorbēre.

tottu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Classical Latin tōtus, of uncertain origin.

all of (followed by a cardinal number)
tottu a.etymology: Literally, “all and”. Compare Italian tutti e.

glosses_en: used as an emphasizer; myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves

alicunu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *alicūnus from Latin aliquī (“some, any”) + ūnus (“one”). Doublet of alcunu and algunu.

alcunu.etymology: Likely a borrowing from Old Italian alcuno. Doublet of alicunu and algunu.

algunu.etymology: Likely a borrowing from Spanish alguno. Doublet of alcunu and alicunu.

indunu-indunu.etymology: Reduplication of indunu, from in d'unu (literally “in one”).

una cun.etymology: From Latin ūnā cum, from ūnā (“together”), inflected form of ūnus (“one”).

faddire.etymology: From Old Sardinian fallire, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.

trabagliare.etymology: From Old Catalan trabaylar and/or Italian travagliare, either way ultimately from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre.

vortare.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.

istunda.etymology: Of Germanic origin, compare Corsican stonda.

iscaressere.etymology:
Borrowed from Old Spanish escaecer (“forget”), from Vulgar Latin *excadescere.
Far more common in Campidanese than in northern dialects, which favour the Italian borrowing ismenticare.

gosare.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish gozar. More-or-less a doublet of the synonym godire, which arrived via Italian.

monzu.etymology: Borrowed from Old Catalan monjo. Doublet of monacu, the native form.

monacu.etymology:
Originally inherited from Latin monachus (both in the form monacu and the others listed above), then later displaced by the doublet monzu, a borrowing from Catalan.
In modern times the specific form monacu has returned as a borrowing of Ita

glosses_en: to scare something away by shouting

abbaidare.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Old Italian agguaitare, aguaitare, from Old French aguaitier, agaitier (“to watch, survey, keep watch”), derived from gaitier (“to watch, survey”). Compare Nuorese abbadiare, abbaitare.

glosses_en: a male given name from Late Latin, equivalent to Campidanese Gavinu, Sassarese Gabinu, Gallurese Gavinu, or Italian Gavino; diminutive form Bainzu
a male given name from Late Latin, equivalent to Campidanese Gavinu, Sassarese Gabinu, Gallurese Gavinu, or Italian Gavino; diminutive form Gabinzu
Gabinu.etymology: From Late Latin Gabīnus, possibly derived from Classical Latin Gabiī, name of an ancient city in Latium.

glosses_en: a diminutive of the male given name Gabinu, from Late Latin, equivalent to Nuorese Gabinzu, Campidanese Baìngiu, Sassarese Bainzu, or Gallurese Baignu
Bainzu.etymology: From Late Latin Gabīnius, derived from Gabīnus, possibly derived from Classical Latin Gabiī, name of an ancient city in Latium.

istade.etymology: Inherited from Latin aestās, aestātem (“summer”), from a reshaping of Proto-Italic *aissāts, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éydʰ-teh₂t-s, derived from the root *h₂eydʰ- (“to ignite; fire”). Compare Campidanese stadi.

ammentare.etymology: Derived from a- (“to, towards”) + mente (“mind”) + -are (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix). Compare Campidanese ammentai.

ammentai.etymology: Derived from a- (“to, towards”) + mente (“mind”) + -ai (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix). Compare Logudorese and Nuorese ammentare.

inoghe.etymology: Suggested to derive from Latin in hoc (“in this (place)”), in contrast with other modern Romance derivations from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc (Italian qui, Spanish aquí, etc.), *eccum hāc (Italian qua, Spanish acá, etc.), and attested Latin ecc

inoche.etymology: Suggested to derive from Latin in hoc (“in this (place)”), in contrast with other modern Romance derivations from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc (Italian qui, Spanish aquí, etc.), *eccum hāc (Italian qua, Spanish acá, etc.), and attested Latin ecc

èsseri.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse.

glosses_en: a kind of luminary or candle left at a grave or similar site, to honor the deceased or a saint

tzerpellucu.etymology: Compare Sardinian cerpiu ("insect"), and figurative use of regional variant Sardinian tzirpiliu ("insect, small child").

belme.etymology: From Latin vermem. Cognates include Italian verme, Spanish verme.

glosses_en: A plum that has not matured, or is shrunken, overly ripe.

glosses_en: handful (of grains or seeds collected in a harvest)
mannuciu.etymology: From Late Latin manuculus (“handful”), from Latin manipulus. Related to Spanish manojo (“handful, bunch”).

frustigalla.etymology: Likely related to Latin fūstis (“stick, club”). Compare Italian fusto (“trunk, stem”) and Spanish fuste (“wood, stick”). Compare Romanian fuscel.

glosses_en: a large knife for use in the kitchen

rasogia.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rāsōria, from the plural of Late Latin rāsōrium (reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun).

rennu.etymology: From Classical Latin rēgnum (“royal power; kingship”), derived from rēx (“king”).

glosses_en: a male given name from Late Latin, equivalent to Logudorese Gabinu, Sassarese Gabinu, or Italian Gavino; diminutive form Baìngiu
Gavinu.etymology: From Late Latin Gabīnus, possibly derived from Classical Latin Gabiī, name of an ancient city in Latium.

Baìngiu.etymology: From Late Latin Gabīnius, derived from Gabīnus, possibly derived from Classical Latin Gabiī, name of an ancient city in Latium.

Gabinzu.etymology: From Late Latin Gabīnius, derived from Gabīnus, possibly derived from Classical Latin Gabiī, name of an ancient city in Latium.

giosso.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iosso, from Classical Latin deorsum. Cognate with Italian giù and Sicilian jusu.

domìniga.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”).

glosses_en: United States (a country in North America)
Istados Unidos.etymology: From istados + unidos. Calque of English United States.

subile.etymology: With an epenthetic -b- (developed through influence from the rounded vowel -u-), from Classical Latin suīle (“pigsty”), derived from sūs (“pig”) + -īle (suffix denoting enclosures for animals). Compare Logudorese suile, dialectal Sassarese

annuzare.etymology: Borrowed from Old Catalan anujar, from Late Latin inodiāre.

glosses_en: obsolete form of cussu (“this, these (referring to an object close to the addressee)”)

issoru.etymology: From Latin ipsorum, genitive masculine of ipse.

brèmmini.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Romance *verminem, from Latin vermis.

glosses_en: initialism of Istados Unidos de Amèrica (= United States of America): a country in North America: USA
